definition: A randomised experiment comparing two variants, where randomisation makes the groups comparable so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the change.
Classifying items (usually SKUs) by their share of total value, so planning effort concentrates on the ~20% that drive ~80% of value.
The share of predictions that are correct. Misleading whenever classes are imbalanced.
The carryover effect of advertising, where spend in one period continues to influence sales in later periods.
A forecasting model combining autoregression, differencing for stationarity, and moving-average error terms.
Average revenue per user, over a stated period.
Assigning credit for a conversion across the marketing touchpoints that preceded it. A heuristic allocation, not a causal measurement.
Area under the precision-recall curve. The preferred ranking metric when positives are rare.
Area under the ROC curve: the probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative.
Training models on bootstrap samples and averaging them to reduce variance. The basis of random forests.
The underlying prevalence of an outcome in the population. Ignoring it is the base rate fallacy.
The rule for inverting a conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).
Estimating uncertainty by repeatedly resampling the observed data with replacement.
The amplification of demand variability as it moves upstream through a supply chain.
Customer acquisition cost: fully loaded acquisition spend divided by new customers acquired.
Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies — among items scored 0.3, about 30% should be positive.
DIO + DSO − DPO: the days between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.
The result that the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as n grows, whatever the population's shape.
The share of customers lost during a period, measured against the count at the start of that period.
Customer lifetime value: the total gross profit a customer is expected to generate.
Grouping users by when they started and tracking each group separately, separating product quality from acquisition volume.
A range built so that, over repeated sampling, a stated share of such intervals would contain the true parameter.
A third variable that causes both of two correlated variables, creating an association that is not causal.
Revenue minus variable costs — the amount each additional sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit.
A measure of linear association between two variables, ranging from −1 to +1.
A six-phase analytics project lifecycle: business understanding, data understanding, preparation, modelling, evaluation, deployment.
Repeatedly splitting data into train and validation folds to estimate out-of-sample performance more stably.
Tufte's principle that the proportion of a chart's ink devoted to representing data should be maximised.
Summarising what happened — counts, sums, rates and trends.
Determining why something happened, usually through disciplined segmentation.
A quasi-experimental method comparing the before/after change in a treated group against an untreated control group.
The number of features describing each observation. High dimensionality makes distance-based methods less reliable.
Economic order quantity: the order size that minimises combined ordering and holding costs.
The percentage change in one quantity per percentage change in another; price elasticity of demand is the common case.
The probability-weighted average of possible outcomes.
The row multiplication that occurs when joining on a key that is not unique, silently inflating aggregates.
A score for how much a model relies on each input. Predictive, never causal.
The share of ordered units shipped from available stock.
Measuring conversion through sequential stages to locate where users drop out.
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
An ensemble method that builds trees sequentially, each fitting the errors of the ensemble so far.
What one row of a table or result represents. Most silent analytical errors are grain errors.
(Revenue − cost of goods sold) ÷ revenue. The fastest read on a business model.
Non-constant error variance in a regression, typically appearing as a funnel-shaped residual plot.
A framework for judging whether observed data is plausible under a null hypothesis of no effect.
A classification problem where one outcome is much rarer than the other, making accuracy misleading.
The causal effect of an activity, measured by comparing against a holdout that did not receive it.
A measurement scale with equal intervals but an arbitrary zero, so differences are meaningful and ratios are not.
A clustering algorithm that assigns points to the nearest of k centroids and iterates until assignments stabilise.
A metric a team has agreed to be measured against, as distinct from a metric that is merely tracked.
Information in training data that would not be available at prediction time, producing inflated offline performance.
A right-skewed, strictly positive distribution whose logarithm is normal. The default shape of business data.
A model of a binary outcome, linear in the log-odds and bounded between 0 and 1.
Mean absolute percentage error. Scale-free but undefined near zero and biased toward under-forecasting.
Mean absolute scaled error: forecast MAE divided by naive MAE. Below 1 beats the naive baseline.
Mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive — the property a good issue tree needs.
The middle value of a sorted dataset; the robust measure of centre for skewed business data.
Minimum detectable effect: the smallest difference an experiment is designed to detect.
Strong correlation among predictors, which destabilises individual coefficients without harming prediction.
Net revenue retention: revenue from an existing cohort versus its original revenue, including expansion. Above 100% means growth without new customers.
Unordered categories, supporting counts and modes but no arithmetic.
The default assumption of no effect or no difference, which a test attempts to reject.
The exponentiated coefficient of a logistic regression — the multiplicative change in odds per unit of the predictor.
Ordered categories whose intervals are not known to be equal, supporting medians but not strictly means.
On-time in-full: the share of orders delivered complete and on schedule.
Fitting noise in the training data, producing strong training performance and poor generalisation.
The probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
The empirical pattern that a small share of inputs accounts for most of the output — the 80/20 rule.
Repeatedly checking an experiment and stopping when it reaches significance, which inflates the false positive rate.
The value below which a given share of observations falls. p95 is often more decision-relevant than the mean.
The distribution of event counts in a fixed interval at a constant rate, where mean equals variance.
The probability of detecting an effect that genuinely exists; conventionally targeted at 80%.
Of the cases flagged positive, the share that really were positive.
Estimating unknown or future values from historical patterns.
Recommending an action, usually by combining a prediction with costs and constraints.
Structuring communication answer-first, with supporting arguments beneath it.
The share of variance in the outcome explained by a regression model. Not a measure of correctness.
An ensemble of decorrelated decision trees trained on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets.
A scale with equal intervals and a true zero, so ratios and percentage changes are meaningful.
Of all genuine positives, the share the model successfully identified.
The tendency of extreme observations to be followed by more typical ones, often mistaken for the effect of an intervention.
Segmenting customers by recency, frequency and monetary value of their purchases.
Return on ad spend: attributed revenue divided by advertising spend. Ignores margin.
Buffer inventory held to absorb variability in demand and lead time at a chosen service level.
Systematic error from a sample that does not represent the population. No sample size fixes it.
Regular, fixed-period variation in a time series, such as weekly or annual cycles.
Dividing customers into groups that can be identified, are substantial, respond differently, and can be acted on.
Testing how much a conclusion changes when key assumptions are varied.
Per-prediction feature attributions with a game-theoretic basis, used to explain complex models.
A measure of clustering quality comparing within-cluster to nearest-cluster distances.
When a relationship present in every subgroup reverses once the groups are pooled, due to differing group mixes.
Asymmetry in a distribution. Right skew, with mean above median, is the norm for business data.
Sample ratio mismatch: an experiment's traffic split differing from its intended allocation, indicating a defect.
The standard deviation of a sample statistic's sampling distribution; for the mean it is σ/√n.
A time series whose statistical properties do not change over time — a requirement for ARIMA.
Drawing conclusions from surviving cases while the failures are absent from the data.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis — a false positive.
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis — a false negative.
A number that rises regardless of performance and implies no action — typically a cumulative counter.
Decomposing a gap against plan into price, volume and mix contributions.
A SQL function computing a value across related rows without collapsing them into one.
Capital tied up in inventory and receivables, which consumes cash as a business grows.
